arguments.value: This agreement says AIG must keep its Delaware life insurance subsidiary adequately capitalized. If the subsidiary’s capital falls below a set minimum percentage of required capital, AIG must contribute cash, securities, or other qualifying assets to restore capital levels. If the subsidiary’s capital is above the minimum, the company may pay ordinary dividends up to the amount needed to bring capital back down to the target level, subject to law and approvals. The minimum percentage is initially 350% of the company’s risk-based capital and can be reviewed and adjusted over time based on rating agency and regulatory standards. The agreement sets timing rules for contributions and dividends, requires compliance with law and board approvals, and allows policyholders to enforce certain rights if the company fails to do so. It is not a guarantee of the company’s debts, does not give policyholders rights against AIG’s assets, lasts indefinitely unless terminated by AIG under limited conditions or after a sale, is governed by New York law, and replaced an earlier 1991 capital maintenance letter agreement.
